01

EC2 + Auto Scaling

Compute that grows and heals itself

EC2 gives you resizable virtual servers in the cloud. Auto Scaling keeps a healthy number of those servers running, adds capacity when demand rises, removes it when demand falls, and automatically replaces instances that fail.

  • EC2 — virtual machines; you pick instance type, OS, storage (EBS), and networking. Access is controlled by Security Groups, Key Pairs and IAM roles.
  • Launch Template defines how new instances are built (AMI, type, user-data, SG).
  • Auto Scaling Group (ASG) holds min / desired / max counts and spreads instances across AZs.
  • Scaling policies (target-tracking / step) react to CloudWatch alarms; health checks replace unhealthy nodes.
  • Combine EC2 + ASG + Load Balancer for a highly available, fault-tolerant tier.
Architecture
flowchart LR
    U["Users"] --> ALB["Application Load Balancer"]
    subgraph ASG["Auto Scaling Group  (min 2 / max 8)"]
      direction TB
      E1["EC2 - AZ-a"]
      E2["EC2 - AZ-b"]
      E3["EC2 - scaled out"]
    end
    ALB --> E1
    ALB --> E2
    ALB --> E3
    CW["CloudWatch alarm - CPU 60%"] --> SP["Scaling policy"]
    SP --> ASG
STAR interview answer
S
SituationA retail checkout service ran on a fixed pool of EC2 instances. During flash sales, CPU saturated, requests timed out, and scaling the fleet by hand was far too slow to catch the spike.
T
TaskMake the compute tier elastic and self-healing so it absorbs traffic surges automatically, without paying for peak capacity around the clock.
A
ActionI built a launch template with a pre-baked AMI to cut boot time, placed the instances behind an ALB across two AZs, and created an ASG (min 2, desired 2, max 8). I attached a target-tracking policy at 60% CPU plus a step policy for sharp spikes, and tied health checks to the ALB so failed nodes were replaced automatically.
R
ResultThe tier absorbed roughly 5x peak traffic with zero manual intervention, checkout error rate dropped to near zero, unhealthy instances self-healed, and scaling in during off-peak cut steady-state compute cost by about a third.
02

VPC + Networking

Your own isolated, layered network

A VPC is a logically isolated virtual network you fully control — IP ranges, subnets, routing and security. It is the foundation every other AWS resource sits inside.

  • Subnets split the VPC into public (internet-facing) and private (backend) tiers, ideally across multiple AZs.
  • Internet Gateway gives public subnets internet access; NAT Gateway lets private subnets reach out without being reachable.
  • Route tables decide where traffic goes (local, IGW, NAT, peering).
  • Security Group = stateful firewall on the instance; NACL = stateless firewall on the subnet.
  • VPC Endpoints reach S3/DynamoDB and other services privately, keeping traffic off the public internet.
Architecture
flowchart LR
    NET["Internet"] --> IGW["Internet Gateway"]
    IGW --> PUB["Public subnet - ALB / NAT"]
    PUB --> APP["Private subnet - App"]
    APP --> DB["Private subnet - Data"]
    APP --> NAT["NAT Gateway"] --> IGW
    APP -. gateway endpoint .-> S3["S3 / DynamoDB"]
STAR interview answer
S
SituationA startup ran everything in a single public subnet — even the databases had public IPs. A security review flagged the flat, internet-exposed network as a major risk.
T
TaskRe-architect into a secure, multi-tier VPC that enforces least privilege and passes the audit.
A
ActionI designed a 10.0.0.0/16 VPC with public subnets for the ALB and NAT and private subnets for app and data, spread across two AZs. Public egress went through an IGW, private egress through a NAT Gateway. I chained Security Groups (ALB to app to DB only), added NACLs as a subnet-level guardrail, created S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints, and turned on VPC Flow Logs.
R
ResultDatabases were no longer reachable from the internet, the audit passed, endpoint traffic cut NAT data-processing cost, and Flow Logs gave us the forensic visibility we'd been missing.
03

Load Balancer + API Gateway

The front door for traffic and APIs

Elastic Load Balancing spreads incoming traffic across healthy targets. API Gateway is a managed front door for APIs that adds auth, throttling, caching and versioning at scale.

  • ALB (Layer 7) routes on path / host / headers — best for web apps and microservices.
  • NLB (Layer 4) handles extreme-performance TCP/UDP workloads.
  • LB features: health checks, SSL/TLS termination, sticky sessions, cross-zone balancing.
  • API Gateway adds IAM/Cognito auth, API keys, throttling, caching, stages/versions and WAF.
  • Use VPC Link to let API Gateway reach private backends.
Architecture
flowchart LR
    U["Users"] --> ALB["ALB - L7 path/host routing"]
    ALB --> TG1["Target group - /cart"]
    ALB --> TG2["Target group - /orders"]
    C["API clients / partners"] --> AGW["API Gateway - auth, throttle, cache"]
    AGW --> L["Lambda"]
    AGW --> VL["VPC Link -> private service"]
STAR interview answer
S
SituationWe were breaking a monolith into microservices and also needed to expose a public partner API — but there was no clean way to route by path or to protect the API from abuse.
T
TaskRoute traffic to the right service and expose a secured, rate-limited API to external partners.
A
ActionI put an ALB in front of the services with path- and host-based rules to separate target groups, terminated TLS at the ALB with an ACM certificate, and kept sticky sessions only where needed. For the partner API I used API Gateway with usage plans and API keys, request throttling, response caching, WAF, and Cognito/IAM auth, reaching private services over a VPC Link.
R
ResultRouting became clean and declarative, TLS was offloaded from the app, partner abuse was throttled at the edge, and response caching cut backend load by roughly 40%.
04

CloudFront + Route 53

Global delivery and smart DNS

CloudFront is a CDN that caches content at 400+ edge locations for low latency. Route 53 is a highly available DNS service with health checks and advanced routing policies.

  • CloudFront caches static and dynamic content near users; supports HTTPS, signed URLs, and Origin Access Control for S3.
  • Route 53 routing policies: simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity, multivalue.
  • Health checks + failover route users away from an unhealthy region automatically.
  • Together: Route 53 finds the right destination, CloudFront delivers it fastest.
  • Enable DNSSEC and use OAC to lock the S3 origin to CloudFront only.
Architecture
flowchart LR
    U["Users - global"] --> R53["Route 53 - latency / failover"]
    R53 --> CF["CloudFront - edge cache"]
    CF --> O1["Origin - region A (S3/ALB)"]
    R53 -. failover .-> O2["Standby origin - region B"]
STAR interview answer
S
SituationA global single-page app was served from S3 in one region. Users in APAC and Europe saw high latency, and a regional issue could take the whole site down.
T
TaskCut global latency and add DNS-level failover so a single region can't be a single point of failure.
A
ActionI fronted the S3 origin with CloudFront using Origin Access Control, cached assets at the edge, and enforced HTTPS. In Route 53 I created an alias to CloudFront with latency-based routing across two regional origins, added health checks with automatic failover to a standby, and enabled DNSSEC.
R
ResultTime-to-first-byte dropped sharply for international users, origin load fell as the edge served most requests, and during a later regional incident DNS failover kept the site available with no manual action.
05

RDS + DynamoDB

Pick the right database for the job

RDS is a managed relational database (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Aurora and more) that handles backups, patching and high availability. DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless NoSQL store with single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale.

  • RDS: Multi-AZ for automatic failover, read replicas for read scaling, automated backups + point-in-time recovery.
  • DynamoDB: serverless, horizontal scaling, key-value/document, global tables for multi-region.
  • Choose RDS for complex relational data and ACID transactions; DynamoDB for large-scale, high-throughput, low-latency access.
  • RDS scales vertically; DynamoDB scales horizontally by partition.
  • Encrypt at rest on both; use least-privilege IAM and Security Groups.
Architecture
flowchart LR
    APP["Application"] --> SG["Security Group"]
    SG --> P["RDS primary - Multi-AZ"]
    P -. sync .-> STB["Standby - AZ-b"]
    P --> RR["Read replicas - reporting"]
    APP --> DDB["DynamoDB table"]
    DDB --> PA["Partitions - auto scale"]
STAR interview answer
S
SituationHeavy reporting queries were hitting the primary transactional database and slowing checkout, and a session/cart store living on the same SQL database couldn't keep up during traffic spikes.
T
TaskProtect transactional performance and give the cart a scalable, low-latency store.
A
ActionI enabled Multi-AZ on RDS for fast failover, added read replicas and pointed all analytics and reporting at them, and tightened automated backups with point-in-time recovery. I moved sessions and cart data to DynamoDB with on-demand capacity and a deliberate key design, added auto-scaling/DAX on the hot path, and encrypted both at rest.
R
ResultCheckout latency recovered immediately, failover tested in seconds, the cart handled spikes at single-digit-millisecond latency, and moving reporting to replicas removed the primary-database bottleneck.
06

Lambda + Serverless

Run code, not servers

Lambda runs your code in response to events without any servers to provision or manage. It scales automatically and you pay only for the compute time you actually use.

  • Components: function, handler (entry point), runtime, IAM role, triggers, layers, environment variables.
  • Event-driven: invoked by S3, API Gateway, DynamoDB Streams, EventBridge, SNS/SQS and more.
  • Built-in auto-scaling and high availability; pay-per-invocation.
  • Mind cold starts — use provisioned concurrency on latency-sensitive paths.
  • Serverless ≠ no servers — the servers are just managed by AWS, not by you.
Architecture
flowchart LR
    S3E["S3 event"] --> L["AWS Lambda function"]
    AGW["API Gateway"] --> L
    EB["EventBridge / DynamoDB Streams"] --> L
    L --> DDB["DynamoDB"]
    L --> OUT["S3 / SNS / SQS"]
    L -. failures .-> DLQ["Dead-letter queue"]
STAR interview answer
S
SituationAn image-processing pipeline ran on always-on EC2 workers. They sat idle most of the day but were still under-provisioned during upload spikes.
T
TaskReplace the fleet with something that scales to zero and still absorbs bursts.
A
ActionI wired an S3 put-event to a Lambda that generated thumbnails and wrote metadata to DynamoDB. I used layers for shared libraries, tuned memory and timeout, gave it a least-privilege execution role, added a dead-letter queue with retries, and put provisioned concurrency on the hot path to eliminate cold starts.
R
ResultCompute cost dropped dramatically since we paid only per invocation, upload bursts were absorbed automatically, and we removed all server patching and scaling overhead.
07

SQS + SNS — Event-Driven

Decouple, buffer, and fan out

SQS is a managed message queue for reliable point-to-point processing; SNS is pub/sub messaging that fans one message out to many subscribers. Together they enable scalable, reliable, event-driven systems.

  • SQS: decouples producers and consumers, at-least-once delivery, standard & FIFO queues, long polling, visibility timeout, DLQ.
  • SNS: one-to-many pub/sub, multiple protocols (SQS, Lambda, email, HTTP), message filtering, cross-region.
  • Pattern: publish once to SNS, fan out to several SQS queues, each processed independently.
  • Use FIFO when order matters; DLQ for poison messages; filtering so subscribers get only relevant events.
  • Result: decoupled, scalable, reliable, event-driven architecture.
Architecture
flowchart LR
    SRC["Order service"] --> SNS["SNS topic - order-events"]
    SNS --> Q1["SQS - inventory"] --> W1["Worker"]
    SNS --> Q2["SQS - notifications"] --> W2["Email / SMS"]
    SNS --> Q3["SQS - analytics"] --> W3["Consumer"]
    Q1 -. poison .-> DLQ["Dead-letter queue"]
STAR interview answer
S
SituationThe order service called inventory, email and analytics synchronously. If any one downstream was slow or down, the whole checkout failed.
T
TaskDecouple the flow so an order is accepted instantly and each downstream processes independently and reliably.
A
ActionOn each new order I published to an SNS topic and fanned it out to separate SQS queues for inventory, notifications and analytics, each with its own consumer. I used a FIFO queue where ordering mattered, tuned long polling and visibility timeout, added DLQs for poison messages, and applied message filtering so each subscriber only received relevant events.
R
ResultCheckout became instant and resilient — a downstream outage no longer failed orders because messages buffered and retried — and we later added new consumers with zero changes to the producer.
08

CloudWatch + CloudTrail

See it, alert on it, audit it

CloudWatch collects metrics, logs and events and lets you alarm and visualize them. CloudTrail records every API call for governance and auditing. Together they give you observability plus a full audit trail.

  • CloudWatch: metrics, alarms, dashboards, centralized Logs, Logs Insights, Container Insights.
  • CloudTrail: records API calls (who did what), stores to S3, supports multi-region/multi-account trails.
  • Flow: CloudTrail records API calls, CloudWatch Logs stores & analyzes, alarms trigger actions and notify via SNS.
  • Set meaningful alarms to avoid alert fatigue; keep logs centralized and searchable.
  • Monitoring isn't just collecting data — it's using it to take action and improve systems.
Architecture
flowchart LR
    RES["EC2 / RDS / Lambda / ALB"] --> CW["CloudWatch - metrics & logs"]
    CW --> AL["Alarm - CPU / 5XX / latency"]
    AL --> SNS["SNS"] --> N["Slack / PagerDuty / Email"]
    AL --> LR["Lambda - auto remediation"]
    RES --> CT["CloudTrail - API audit"] --> S3["S3 - long-term store"]
STAR interview answer
S
SituationCustomers were reporting incidents before we noticed them. There was no proactive alerting and no reliable record of who changed what in the account.
T
TaskBuild proactive monitoring and alerting, plus a compliance-grade audit trail.
A
ActionI created CloudWatch alarms on CPU, 5XX and latency that paged Slack and PagerDuty through SNS, built per-service dashboards, centralized logs with Logs Insights, and enabled Container Insights for EKS. I turned on a multi-region CloudTrail writing to S3 with log-file integrity validation, wired critical events to alarms, and added Lambda auto-remediation for a couple of well-understood conditions.
R
ResultMean time to detect and recover dropped sharply, we caught issues before customers did, and the full CloudTrail audit trail satisfied compliance and made post-incident RCA straightforward.

StorageS3 — object · EBS — block · EFS — file · Glacier — archival
DatabaseRDS — managed relational · DynamoDB — NoSQL · Aurora — AWS relational · ElastiCache — in-memory
Networking & CDNVPC — private network · Route 53 — DNS · CloudFront — CDN · ELB — load balancing
IntegrationSQS — message queue · SNS — notifications · EventBridge — event bus · API Gateway — APIs

Memory trick — “CES + N + D + M + S” Compute · Edge · Storage  +  Networking  +  Database  +  Monitoring  +  Security — walk these seven buckets and you can place almost any AWS service on the spot.

High-yield Q&A

Security Group vs NACL
SG is stateful and attached to an instance/ENI; return traffic is automatically allowed. NACL is stateless, attached at the subnet level, evaluates numbered rules, and you must allow return traffic explicitly.
ALB vs NLB
ALB works at Layer 7 with content/path/host routing for web apps and APIs. NLB works at Layer 4 for extreme-performance TCP/UDP with static IPs and ultra-low latency.
Stop vs Terminate (EC2)
Stop keeps the EBS root volume and you can start again later (you keep data, pay for storage). Terminate deletes the instance and, by default, the root volume.
Scale Up vs Scale Out
Scale up = bigger instance (vertical). Scale out = more instances (horizontal). Auto Scaling does scale-out, which is more resilient and elastic.
SQS vs SNS
SQS is a pull-based queue for decoupled point-to-point processing. SNS is push-based pub/sub that fans one message out to many subscribers. They're often combined (SNS fan-out to SQS).
Multi-AZ vs Read Replica (RDS)
Multi-AZ is for high availability — a synchronous standby for automatic failover. Read replicas are for read scaling — asynchronous copies you send read traffic to.
Gateway vs Interface Endpoint
Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) are free and use route-table entries. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) create an ENI in your subnet for most other services.
How do you make an app highly available?
Multiple AZs, Auto Scaling behind a load balancer, Multi-AZ databases, health checks with automatic failover, and stateless app tiers with shared session/cart stores.
